prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of prose and poetry in Romanian, centred on large-scale novels, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an expansive, densely patterned metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: Mircea Cărtărescu alone, with a citation for the whole oeuvre. The reasons are the work, not the unanimous openings, which I do not count as evidence. On public knowledge of the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid, his voice is recognisable at once. Dense, recursive, image-driven prose makes memory, the body, dream and cosmology into one imaginative system, and the poetry supplies its lyric and metaphoric base. The chair asked which book should test the claim of widening rather than repetition. I would test it by reading Solenoid against Blinding. The question is whether the later book reorganises the earlier materials into a different structure and a different intellectual argument, or only restages them at greater length. From public description I lean toward the first reading, but I have not verified it by reading and I hold that lean provisionally. On citation scope, I have moved partly toward Olsson and Palm. The citation should rest its weight on the major prose and name the poetry as origin and companion strand, because translated coverage of the poetry and early work is uneven and a claim for the whole must not outrun what we can assess. I still prefer to name 'prose and poetry' and not prose alone. A prize is for a whole authorship, and a citation that drops the lyric base would misdescribe how the prose is made. The attribution is clean: one writer, one language, with no dependence on national or political symbolism.
statement.case_against: I will state the strongest case against my own choice, since the chair asked who will do so. First, the achievement lies largely in Romanian density, wordplay and rhythm, and a committee reading in translation may be judging a partly flattened text. If so, the confident language of unmistakable voice may reflect the reputation of the books and the architecture visible through translation, not the sentences themselves. Second, the shared motifs of body, childhood, dream and cosmos across very long books may be a closed circuit, and scale can be mistaken for depth. Third, six identical first places in the openings may mean we have scrutinised the shared reservations less than a divided committee would. If a reader of the Romanian showed that the prose is materially weaker in the later large books, or that the translations misrepresent the style, I would weigh that seriously and the alternatives more heavily. I have no such evidence now.

responses.point: Olsson treats repetition versus deepening as the real test of this candidacy, saying the answer must come from the books and not from their reputation. He would ground the citation mainly in the major prose, with the poetry as a related strand.
responses.response: I agree that the books must settle the repetition question and that I cannot settle it from reputation. That is why I would name Solenoid against Blinding as the test. On scope I have moved toward him. The citation should weight the major prose and treat the poetry as origin and companion strand, because the poetry's translated coverage does not support a claim of equal weight. I still keep 'prose and poetry' in the wording and do not narrow it to prose alone, since the lyric base is part of how the prose is made. I read that as a drafting difference, not a difference of judgment.

responses.point: Palm argues that Cărtărescu's effect rests more on large-scale architecture and imagery, which she thinks survive translation better than Michon's syntax and cadence. She says this is a judgment about the type of effect, not verified knowledge of the translations.
responses.response: I find this a useful distinction and partly accept it. Imagery and structural design probably do travel better than cadence. But it does not remove the translation uncertainty. Much of what makes the prose recognisable to me may be rhythm and syntactic patterning, and that is exactly what a structural argument would not preserve. I would therefore treat her point as lowering the risk, not removing it. It is also why I would put weight on any assessment by a reader of the Romanian, as the chair suggests, before relying on the architecture argument alone. On Can Xue, I accept her reading that the method matters and that more evidence of development is needed, and I made the same point in round 1.

responses.point: Mattson reads motif recurrence in the large works as the means by which the project accumulates meaning, not as narrowness, while saying it should be tested against specific books. She also keeps Michon as first alternative, citing intensity of voice against a small corpus.
responses.response: Her reading of recurrence as accumulation is the one I lean toward, and her insistence on testing it against specific books is right. I would not claim more than a lean. On Michon, I ranked him lowest in my opening, and the discussion has made me value the concentration of his voice more than my ranking showed. My reasons for not putting him ahead were corpus size and the fact that I cannot judge cadence in French translation. They were not doubts about the voice. I do not move him above Cărtărescu, and I agree with her that a citation for Michon would have to say precisely what is honoured. I do not replace my alternatives with him, because my alternatives answer a different chair question: what to advance if Romanian cannot be judged, which would put weight on a different set of criteria.

responses.point: Carlberg did not rank Can Xue in her top eight because she cannot tell from the translated selection whether the method develops or repeats. She would want the coverage question settled before moving her up. On Carson, she says a citation would have to centre on poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal.
responses.response: I accept that criticism of my Can Xue ranking. I ranked her second for the rigour and rarity of the method, but I have been candid that I cannot show development across the oeuvre from the translations. For that reason I keep her as an alternative and not as a preferred choice, and I would not ask the committee to rely on my rank alone. On Carson, her proposed scope seems to me the workable one: poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal, with the translations and book-object effects set aside as supporting context. That answers part of the chair's question. It does not answer whether the genre-crossing is the achievement or only a vehicle for it, and I still find that open. It is why Carson stays second among my alternatives.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says Cărtărescu's major books reorganise the same materials at different scales and in different forms, which he reads as development. He also discloses thematic proximity to Central Europe and says he tried to discount any familiarity effect.
responses.response: I share his reading of the large books as reorganising the same materials, and I note that it rests on public knowledge, as his own statement says. His disclosure seems to me the right way to handle proximity. A familiarity effect is a real risk for a candidate whose themes are close to a member's own concerns, and I would apply the same discipline to myself. My confidence in this case should be as strong as the evidence for the books and no stronger.

uncertainties: How much of the Romanian patterning, wordplay and rhythm reaches readers in translation. I have not read the originals, have not independently verified any text, and judge from public knowledge and translation.
Whether Solenoid deepens and widens the project begun in Blinding or restages it at greater length. I lean toward development, but this has not been tested against the books themselves.
How far the translated poetry and early work can support a whole-oeuvre citation. This is why I would weight the citation toward the major prose.
Whether Can Xue's method develops across a large, only partly translated oeuvre. My alternative ranking of her is provisional on that point.
Whether Carson's genre-crossing is the literary achievement or a vehicle for it, and whether a citation can fix her scope without relying on book design, translation or scholarship.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I have no documented personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My ties to committee colleagues are collegial service only, including joining the committee for 2021 alongside Mattson. I have said publicly that the Academy has overlooked many significant women's authorships. That is a general statement about the Academy's record and is not a reason for preferring any candidate, including the women on this shortlist, and I have tried to keep it out of my merit assessment. My own practice as a novelist is context only.
